title: Yes, We’re in an AI Bubble. Just Look to 1980s Japan.
gist: Despite Nvidia's spectacular earnings ($60B net profit, $96.22B revenue, $5T+ market cap), the author warns the circular financing between Nvidia and unprofitable customers like OpenAI echoes Japan's late-1980s cross-shareholding bubble—where financing tracked relationships over cash flow—and cautions that Japanese stocks took 34 years to regain their 1989 peak.

themes.theme: Nvidia's earnings and the demand paradox

insights.claim: Nvidia's net profit doubled year-over-year to roughly $60 billion (versus $6.2 billion three years ago) on revenue of $96.22 billion, with a $5 trillion-plus market cap and guidance for a further 70 percent revenue rise next fiscal year.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of Nvidia's dominance and the market's dependence on it—the concentration that makes any AI reversal systemic.
insights.quote: Reported net profit doubled from a year ago to roughly $60 billion, compared with $6.2 billion just three years ago.

insights.claim: The core dilemma is that Nvidia's chips are expensive and in high demand, but its largest customers racing to build data centers are mostly not making money, even as Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are projected to spend $1.5 trillion on data centers this year and next.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: A $1.5T capex boom funded by customers who can't yet monetize AI is the central fragility—watch for capex cuts that would hit Nvidia's revenue.
insights.quote: few of Nvidia’s largest customers that are racing to build these enormously expensive centers are making money, despite their colossal ongoing investments
insights.locator: At first glance, this model sounds perfect.

insights.claim: Nvidia and the four hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft) together constitute around 23 percent of the entire U.S. stock market's worth, per some estimates.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Extreme concentration means an AI repricing would transmit broadly through index funds and retirement accounts, a systemic-risk quantifier.
insights.quote: those four companies, combined with Nvidia, constitute around 23 percent of the country’s entire stock market in terms of worth
insights.locator: This year and next, just four companies

insights.claim: Nvidia has begun co-financing and investing in its largest chip customers—effectively underwriting them, with OpenAI the biggest example—raising the 'incestuousness' of the AI sector as Nvidia becomes the indispensable banker to the customers and data centers it depends on.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Vendor financing that props up demand is a hallmark of late-cycle bubbles—if Nvidia is funding its own revenue, reported growth may be less organic than it appears.
insights.quote: Nvidia becoming the indispensable banker and potential savior to a growing number of AI companies and the data centers that they rely upon
insights.locator: It is precisely the growing incestuousness

insights.claim: Chinese AI companies have turned U.S. export restrictions to their advantage by building far cheaper models on less expensive domestic chips and open-source architecture, undercutting U.S. competitors from a lower cost basis and pushing Nvidia to develop its own open-weight models to compete with pioneers like DeepSeek.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Cheaper Chinese open-source AI threatens the margins of the high-cost U.S. stack Nvidia supports, and Nvidia's own open-weight hedge could cannibalize its big customers.
insights.quote: Chinese AI companies have figured out a way to turn U.S. export restrictions on Nvidia’s chips to their advantage

insights.claim: OpenAI competitor Anthropic has labored to find paying customers for its most advanced models, and analysts note a persistent gap between big tech's data-center spending and the slow profit generation from AI end products.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Weak monetization at the model layer is the demand-side crack that could eventually starve the capex driving Nvidia's sales.
insights.quote: there remains a persistent gap between how much big tech companies are spending on data centers and other computing infrastructure and how slowly profits are being generated
insights.locator: Maybe so, but OpenAI and some of its peers

insights.claim: Japan's late-1980s bubble featured big industrial groups holding shares in each other, cross-financing, and refusing to sell in downturns—making financing a function of business relationships rather than cash flow—an eerie resemblance to Nvidia's circular architecture with its customers today.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The cross-shareholding analogy provides a concrete historical template for how relationship-based financing masks fragility until it snaps.
insights.quote: Financing, in other words, became more a function of business relationships than objective measures such as cash flow
insights.locator: Nonetheless, a central feature of the Japanese economic system

insights.claim: The current S&P forward P/E of roughly 23, though high by U.S. standards, is only about a third of Japan's ratio in December 1989, and the U.S. market has only come close to doubling since 2022 versus Tokyo's 60 percent rise in 1988-1989 alone.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Valuation is elevated but far below Japan's 1989 extreme—suggesting the bubble, if one, may have room to inflate further before bursting.
insights.quote: The market’s present forward price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 23 may be very high by historic U.S. standards, but it is still only about a third of where Japan’s ratio stood in December 1989.
insights.locator: By comparison, the U.S. S&P’s market value

insights.claim: After Japan's securities market burst in December 1989, stock valuations did not regain their peak until February 2024—34 years later—a cautionary benchmark for how long an AI-bubble unwind could take.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: A 34-year recovery underscores that a burst of this kind of relationship-financed bubble can mean a generation of lost returns, not a quick rebound.
insights.quote: it would not be until February 2024—34 years later—that stock valuations there matched their previous peak
insights.locator: The house of cards that Japan’s bubble

insights.claim: Economists sharply disagree on whether AI will pay off, with MIT's Daron Acemoglu estimating it will boost U.S. productivity by less than 1 percent over the next decade while UVA's Anton Korinek says it may radically boost annual GDP growth.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: The wide expert dispersion on AI's real-economy payoff is itself a risk signal—the investment case rests on an unresolved productivity question.
insights.quote: estimate that it will boost U.S. productivity by less than 1 percent over the next decade
